question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasing pain in the right hip for 2 months. The pain is intermittent, presenting at the lateral side of the hip and radiating towards the thigh. It is aggravated while climbing stairs or lying on the right side. Two weeks ago, the patient was treated with a course of oral prednisone for exacerbation of asthma. Her current medications include formoterol-budesonide and albuterol inhalers. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows tenderness to palpation over the upper lateral part of the right thigh. There is no swelling. The patient is placed in the left lateral decubitus position. Abducting the extended right leg against the physician's resistance reproduces the pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the pelvis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Intermittent pain at lateral side of the hip radiating towards the thigh" -> "Aggravated by climbing stairs or lying on the right side" -> "Tenderness to palpation over upper lateral part of the right thigh" -> "Pain reproduced by abducting the extended right leg against resistance" -> "No abnormalities on x-ray of the pelvis" -> "Greater trochanteric pain syndrome" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Course of oral prednisone for exacerbation of asthma two weeks ago" -> "Current medications include formoterol-budesonide and albuterol inhalers" -> "No abnormalities on x-ray of the pelvis" -> "Intermittent pain at lateral side of the hip radiating towards the thigh" -> "Greater trochanteric pain syndrome" -> 90%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of intermittent pain at the lateral side of the hip, aggravated by specific movements, tenderness to palpation, and pain reproduced with abduction against resistance, along with normal x-ray findings, is consistent with Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome. The use of oral prednisone and inhalers for asthma is not directly related to the diagnosis. No evidence paths provide additional relevant information to support the diagnosis of Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome.
analysis: The patient's presentation of intermittent pain at the lateral side of the hip, tenderness to palpation over the upper lateral part of the right thigh, and reproduction of pain with abduction against resistance are classic signs of Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome. The absence of abnormalities on x-ray further supports this diagnosis. Other options like Iliotibial band syndrome and osteoarthritis would typically present differently. Lumbosacral radiculopathy would involve different neurological findings, and osteonecrosis of the femoral head would usually have different risk factors and imaging findings.
